summary.text: 送 means to send or see someone off. Its analyzed construction joins 辶, associated with walking, to 灷 as a proposed sound element; the historical sound match is not independently demonstrated. The modern shape also inspires a gift-carrying mnemonic, but that is not evidence of origin.

formation.text: A proposed phonosemantic compound: 辵 contributes the walking or going sense, while 灷 is assigned a phonetic role in one paleographic analysis. Shuowen instead analyzes the graph as 辵 plus a reduced 㑞; these are historical interpretations, not a settled component identification. The modern idea of a person waving goodbye or carrying a gift is mnemonic, not proof of ancient formation.

components.text: The visible 辶 is the positional form of 辵, associated here with walking. In 送 it contributes the walking or going sense. 辶 is a side form, not a later replacement for 辵.

灷 is identified as the sound element in a proposed analysis of 送. The account describes its bronze form as 廾 with 丨 and decorative dots, and says its small-seal shape was graphically altered. Its comparison with Shuowen’s reduced 㑞 is not independently established.

sound_limitation.text: The analysis assigns 灷 a phonetic role but supplies no historical pronunciation for 灷 to compare with 送. Modern Mandarin readings zhuàn and sòng are available; they do not establish an ancient sound relation, and the supplied Old Chinese reconstruction is for 送 alone.

sound.text: The supplied modern Mandarin readings are zhuàn for 灷 and sòng for 送. This is a current-reading comparison only; it does not demonstrate their historical sound relationship.

history.text: Shuowen glosses 送 as 遣 and analyzes it as 辵 plus a reduced 㑞; it also records a fuller Zhou-script form, 𨕼. This is a historical dictionary account, not independent confirmation that 㑞 was the sound component in the bronze graph.

Another account analyzes a bronze form as 辵 plus 灷 and reports graphic alteration of 灷 in small-seal writing. Chu-slip forms have also been discussed through several possible shape pathways, and one cannot be arranged in a simple linear sequence from shape alone. The available written reports do not settle a single graphic history.

The standard graph uses 辶 as a positional form of 辵; this form contrast does not by itself date the word or its meanings. Although bronze and seal forms are reported, no image was visually inspected, and the earliest surviving form is not independently dated in this evidence.

A bronze graph in one Zhongshan inscription has been read as 朕, “I, my.” That specific reading does not establish that 送 was generally borrowed to write the pronoun, nor does it reveal the name or pronunciation of any object supposedly depicted by the graph.

uncertainties.text: The proposed 灷 analysis and Shuowen’s reduced-㑞 analysis differ. The evidence supports reporting both interpretations but does not resolve their relationship or establish an ancient sound comparison for 灷 and 送.

The received poem quotation and reported bronze examples do not provide a visually inspected glyph or a precise date for the earliest surviving form of 送. A fuller paleographic sequence remains unresolved.

The evidence does not establish a general phonetic-loan history for writing the pronoun 朕 with a graph read as 送 in one inscription. The depicted-object borrowing account lacks evidence for both an identified object and its ancient name or sound.

senses.period: early received Shijing text; composition date unresolved
senses.text: A received poem uses 送 in a context interpreted as accompanying someone to a place. The quotation attests an early sending or accompanying context, but does not settle the exact distinction between accompanying and seeing someone off.

senses.period: Han-dynasty lexicographic record and medieval dictionary record
senses.text: Shuowen glosses 送 as 遣, and the Guangyun record gives the same gloss with a fanqie reading. These attest the gloss in those dictionary records, not when this sense began.
The supplied modern definition includes “give,” but the evidence does not date this use or establish how it developed from the sending sense.

developments.text: The senses are compatible with a broader sending meaning, but the evidence gives no dated transition or proof of a semantic development between them.
The modern gloss “give” is supplied without dated usage evidence establishing when or how it relates to sending or dispatching.

limitations.text: The early received-text quotation does not establish the poem’s composition date or a precise priority among accompanying, seeing off, and sending senses. Dictionary gloss order is not evidence of semantic chronology.

overview.text: 送 means to send or see someone off. Its analyzed form combines 辶, associated with walking, and a proposed sound element, 灷. The common modern idea of carrying a gift is a mnemonic, not a demonstrated ancient picture.

components.text: 辶 is the side form of 辵, associated with walking, and supplies the going idea in this character.
灷 is proposed as the sound element. Its historical sound match with 送 has not been independently demonstrated.

relationships.text: In 送, 辶 is the positional form of 辵 and contributes the walking or going sense.

One paleographic analysis explicitly assigns 灷 the phonetic role in 送. The supplied evidence does not independently demonstrate a historical sound correspondence; modern Mandarin zhuàn and sòng are only current readings, and no comparable supplied Old Chinese reading for 灷 is available.
